grammarPoints.title: N1 は N2 です (Copula & Topic)
grammarPoints.explanation: Used to state that topic N1 equals or is classified as N2 in polite speech. Negative is じゃありません (or ではありません), past is でした.
grammarPoints.pattern: Noun 1 + は + Noun 2 + です

variants.label: Present Affirmative
variants.explanation: Polite affirmative copula in present tense.

examples.japanese: わたしは学生です。
examples.reading: Watashi wa gakusei desu.
examples.meaning: I am a student.

variants.label: Present Negative
variants.explanation: Polite negative copula in present tense.

examples.japanese: わたしは医者じゃありません。
examples.reading: Watashi wa isha ja arimasen.
examples.meaning: I am not a doctor.

variants.label: Past Affirmative
variants.explanation: Polite affirmative copula in past tense.

examples.japanese: 昨日は日曜日でした。
examples.reading: Kinou wa nichiyoubi deshita.
examples.meaning: Yesterday was Sunday.

variants.label: Past Negative
variants.pattern: N + じゃありませんでした
variants.explanation: Polite negative copula in past tense.

examples.japanese: 昨日は休みじゃありませんでした。
examples.reading: Kinou wa yasumi ja arimasen deshita.
examples.meaning: Yesterday was not a holiday.

examples.japanese: わたしは学生です。
examples.reading: Watashi wa gakusei desu.
examples.meaning: I am a student.

examples.japanese: ミラーさんは会社員です。
examples.reading: Miraa-san wa kaishain desu.
examples.meaning: Mr. Miller is a company employee.

grammarPoints.title: 〜ですか (Polite Questions)
grammarPoints.explanation: Adding the sentence-ending particle か to a polite sentence turns it into a question with rising intonation.
grammarPoints.pattern: Sentence + か

variants.label: Yes/No Question
variants.pattern: N1 は N2 ですか
variants.explanation: Standard yes/no question answered with はい or いいえ.

examples.japanese: あなたは学生ですか。
examples.reading: Anata wa gakusei desu ka.
examples.meaning: Are you a student?

examples.japanese: あの人はだれですか。
examples.reading: Ano hito wa dare desu ka.
examples.meaning: Who is that person?

grammarPoints.title: N1 の N2 (Noun Modification & Possession)
grammarPoints.explanation: Connects two nouns where N1 modifies, possesses, or specifies the affiliation/category of N2.
grammarPoints.pattern: Noun 1 + の + Noun 2

variants.label: Possession / Affiliation
variants.explanation: Shows ownership or organization membership.

examples.japanese: これはわたしの本です。
examples.reading: Kore wa watashi no hon desu.
examples.meaning: This is my book.

examples.japanese: わたしはIMCの社員です。
examples.reading: Watashi wa IMC no shain desu.
examples.meaning: I am an employee of IMC.

grammarPoints.title: 〜ます / 〜ました (Polite Verb Conjugation)
grammarPoints.meaning: Polite verb present/future and past forms
grammarPoints.explanation: The polite verb ending used in everyday formal conversation. 〜ます indicates habitual or future actions; 〜ません is negative; 〜ました is past affirmative; 〜ませんでした is past negative.
grammarPoints.pattern: Verb (masu-stem) + ます / ません / ました / ませんでした

variants.label: Present Affirmative (ます)
variants.explanation: Habitual present or future action.

examples.japanese: 毎朝六時に起きます。
examples.reading: Maiasa rokuji ni okimasu.
examples.meaning: I wake up at 6 o'clock every morning.

variants.label: Present Negative (ません)
variants.meaning: do not / will not do V
variants.explanation: Negative habitual or future action.

examples.japanese: 明日働きません。
examples.reading: Ashita hatarakimasen.
examples.meaning: I will not work tomorrow.

variants.label: Past Affirmative (ました)
variants.explanation: Completed action in the past.

examples.japanese: 昨日図書館で勉強しました。
examples.reading: Kinou toshokan de benkyou shimashita.
examples.meaning: I studied at the library yesterday.

variants.label: Past Negative (ませんでした)
variants.explanation: Action that did not take place in the past.

examples.japanese: 昨晩テレビを見ませんでした。
examples.reading: Sakuban terebi wo mimasen deshita.
examples.meaning: I did not watch TV last night.

examples.japanese: 毎日水を飲みます。
examples.reading: Mainichi mizu wo nomimasu.
examples.meaning: I drink water every day.

grammarPoints.title: 〜に〜がいます / あります (Existence)
grammarPoints.explanation: Expresses the existence or presence of people/animals (います) or inanimate objects/plants (あります) at a location marked by に.
grammarPoints.pattern: Place + に + Noun + が + います / あります

variants.label: Animate Existence (います)
variants.pattern: Place + に + Person/Animal + がいます
variants.meaning: There is a person/animal at Place
variants.explanation: Used for living, moving beings (people, animals).

examples.japanese: 部屋に猫がいます。
examples.reading: Heya ni neko ga imasu.
examples.meaning: There is a cat in the room.

variants.label: Inanimate Existence (あります)
variants.pattern: Place + に + Thing + があります
variants.meaning: There is a thing at Place
variants.explanation: Used for non-living things, plants, and places.

examples.japanese: 机の上に本があります。
examples.reading: Tsukue no ue ni hon ga arimasu.
examples.meaning: There is a book on the desk.

examples.japanese: 机の上に本があります。
examples.reading: Tsukue no ue ni hon ga arimasu.
examples.meaning: There is a book on the desk.

grammarPoints.title: 〜てください (Polite Requests)
grammarPoints.explanation: Used to politely ask, instruct, or invite someone to do something by attaching ください to the verb te-form.
grammarPoints.pattern: Verb (te-form) + ください

variants.label: Polite Request
variants.explanation: Polite request using verb te-form.

examples.japanese: ここに名前を書いてください。
examples.reading: Koko ni namae wo kaite kudasai.
examples.meaning: Please write your name here.

examples.japanese: ちょっと待ってください。
examples.reading: Chotto matte kudasai.
examples.meaning: Please wait a moment.

grammarPoints.title: 〜ています (Continuous Action & Resultant State)
grammarPoints.meaning: is doing ~ / is in a state of ~
grammarPoints.explanation: Indicates an action currently in progress or a resultant/habitual state continuing into the present.
grammarPoints.pattern: Verb (te-form) + います

variants.label: Present Progressive
variants.explanation: Ongoing action right now.

examples.japanese: 今雨が降っています。
examples.reading: Ima ame ga futte imasu.
examples.meaning: It is raining right now.

examples.japanese: ミラーさんは今電話をかけています。
examples.reading: Miraa-san wa ima denwa wo kakete imasu.
examples.meaning: Mr. Miller is making a phone call right now.

grammarPoints.title: 〜てもいいです / 〜ても (Permission & Concession)
grammarPoints.explanation: Attaching もいいです to the te-form expresses permission ('you may do ~'); 〜ても alone expresses concession ('even if ~').
grammarPoints.pattern: Verb (te-form) + もいいです

variants.label: Permission (てもいいです)
variants.explanation: Grants or asks for permission.

examples.japanese: 写真を撮ってもいいですか。
examples.reading: Shashin wo totte mo ii desu ka.
examples.meaning: May I take a photograph?

variants.label: Concession (ても)
variants.explanation: States that the main clause holds true even if the condition occurs.

examples.japanese: 雨が降っても、行きます。
examples.reading: Ame ga futtemo, ikimasu.
examples.meaning: Even if it rains, I will go.

examples.japanese: ここに座ってもいいですか。
examples.reading: Koko ni suwatte mo ii desu ka.
examples.meaning: May I sit here?

grammarPoints.title: 〜から (Cause & Reason)
grammarPoints.explanation: Connects two clauses where the first clause states the subjective reason or cause for the second clause.
grammarPoints.pattern: Clause 1 (Reason) + から、Clause 2 (Result)

variants.label: Polite Reason Clause
variants.explanation: Used in polite speech to state a reason.

examples.japanese: 時間がありませんから、タクシーで行きます。
examples.reading: Jikan ga arimasen kara, takushii de ikimasu.
examples.meaning: Because there is no time, I will go by taxi.

examples.japanese: 時間がありませんから、新聞を読みません。
examples.reading: Jikan ga arimasen kara, shinbun wo yomimasen.
examples.meaning: Because I have no time, I don't read the newspaper.

grammarPoints.title: 〜ので (Objective / Polite Reason)
grammarPoints.explanation: Expresses a cause or reason gently and objectively. Frequently used when asking for permission, making excuses, or stating natural consequences.
grammarPoints.pattern: Plain Form (Na-adj/Noun + な) + ので

variants.label: Objective Reason
variants.explanation: Connects a cause to a polite request or natural result.

examples.japanese: 雨が降っているので、出かけません。
examples.reading: Ame ga futte iru node, dekakemasen.
examples.meaning: Because it is raining, I will not go out.

examples.japanese: 用事があるので、先に帰ります。
examples.reading: Youji ga aru node, saki ni kaerimasu.
examples.meaning: Because I have an errand, I'll go home ahead.

grammarPoints.title: 〜ながら (Simultaneous Actions)
grammarPoints.explanation: Attaches to the verb masu-stem to indicate that a single subject performs two actions simultaneously, with the main action in the second verb.
grammarPoints.pattern: Verb 1 (masu-stem) + ながら + Verb 2

variants.label: Simultaneous Action
variants.explanation: V2 is the primary action; V1 is the accompanying action.

examples.japanese: 音楽を聞きながら勉強します。
examples.reading: Ongaku wo kikinagara benkyou shimasu.
examples.meaning: I study while listening to music.

examples.japanese: 働きながら日本語を勉強しています。
examples.reading: Hatarakinagara nihongo wo benkyou shite imasu.
examples.meaning: I am studying Japanese while working.

grammarPoints.title: 〜たら (Conditional If / When)
grammarPoints.explanation: Formed by adding ら to the plain past (ta-form). Expresses hypothetical conditions ('if') or temporal sequence ('when/after').
grammarPoints.pattern: Plain Past (ta-form) + ら、Main Clause

variants.label: Hypothetical Condition
variants.explanation: Expresses a condition and what will be done if it is met.

examples.japanese: 雨が降ったら、行きません。
examples.reading: Ame ga futtara, ikimasen.
examples.meaning: If it rains, I won't go.

examples.japanese: 駅に着いたら、電話してください。
examples.reading: Eki ni tsuitara, denwa shite kudasai.
examples.meaning: When you arrive at the station, please call me.

grammarPoints.title: 〜ば (Conditional Form)
grammarPoints.explanation: Expresses a general, logical, or hypothetical condition where the main clause naturally follows if the condition holds.
grammarPoints.pattern: Verb (ba-form) / i-Adj (ければ)

variants.label: Affirmative Conditional (〜ば)
variants.explanation: Standard conditional form.

examples.japanese: 春になれば、桜が咲きます。
examples.reading: Haru ni nareba, sakura ga sakimasu.
examples.meaning: When/if spring comes, the cherry blossoms bloom.

examples.japanese: 天気がよければ、向こうに島が見えます。
examples.reading: Tenki ga yokereba, mukou ni shima ga miemasu.
examples.meaning: If the weather is good, you can see the island over there.

grammarPoints.title: 〜のに (Concession: Even Though / Despite)
grammarPoints.explanation: Connects two clauses when the actual result in the second clause runs counter to what would naturally be expected from the first clause, often carrying a nuance of surprise or regret.
grammarPoints.pattern: Plain Form (Na-adj/Noun + な) + のに

variants.label: Unexpected Contrast (のに)
variants.explanation: Used when an unexpected result happens.

examples.japanese: 薬を飲んだのに、まだ治りません。
examples.reading: Kusuri wo nonda noni, mada naorimasen.
examples.meaning: Even though I took medicine, I'm still not cured.

examples.japanese: 日曜日なのに、働かなければなりません。
examples.reading: Nichiyoubi na noni, hatarakanakereba narimasen.
examples.meaning: Even though it is Sunday, I have to work.

grammarPoints.title: 可能形 (Potential Verb Form)
grammarPoints.explanation: Expresses ability or possibility. Direct objects normally marked with を are typically marked with が with potential verbs.
grammarPoints.pattern: Noun + が + Potential Verb

variants.label: Can Do (可能・肯定)
variants.explanation: Expresses capability or situational possibility.

examples.japanese: わたしは漢字が読めます。
examples.reading: Watashi wa kanji ga yomemasu.
examples.meaning: I can read kanji.

examples.japanese: わたしは日本語が少し話せます。
examples.reading: Watashi wa nihongo ga sukoshi hanasemasu.
examples.meaning: I can speak a little Japanese.

grammarPoints.title: 受身形 (Passive Verb Form)
grammarPoints.explanation: Indicates that the subject receives an action performed by an agent marked with に.
grammarPoints.pattern: Receiver + は + Actor + に + Passive Verb

variants.label: Direct Passive
variants.pattern: N1 は N2 に V(passive)
variants.explanation: The agent performing the action is marked with に.

examples.japanese: わたしは先生に褒められました。
examples.reading: Watashi wa sensei ni homeraremashita.
examples.meaning: I was praised by the teacher.

examples.japanese: 弟にパソコンを壊されました。
examples.reading: Otouto ni pasokon wo kowasaremashita.
examples.meaning: My computer was broken by my younger brother.

grammarPoints.title: 第1課 • N1 は N2 です — "N1 is N2"
grammarPoints.explanation: The particle は (read "wa") marks the topic of the sentence: what we are talking about. です works like the verb "to be" and always comes last. It is the polite way of stating something about the topic.
grammarPoints.pattern: N1 は N2 です

variants.label: Lesson 1 Pattern
variants.explanation: The particle は (read "wa") marks the topic of the sentence: what we are talking about. です works like the verb "to be" and always comes last. It is the polite way of stating something about the topic.

examples.japanese: 私はマイク・ミラーです。
examples.reading: 私はマイク・ミラーです。
examples.meaning: I am Mike Miller.

examples.japanese: 私は 会社員です。
examples.reading: 私は 会社員です。
examples.meaning: I am a company employee.

examples.japanese: 私はマイク・ミラーです。
examples.reading: 私はマイク・ミラーです。
examples.meaning: I am Mike Miller.

examples.japanese: 私は 会社員です。
examples.reading: 私は 会社員です。
examples.meaning: I am a company employee.

grammarPoints.title: 第1課 • N1 は N2 じゃありません — negation
grammarPoints.japanese: N1 は N2 じゃありません
grammarPoints.explanation: じゃありません is the polite negative of です: "is not / am not". In formal or written contexts ではありません is used instead, with the same meaning.
grammarPoints.pattern: N1 は N2 じゃありません

variants.label: Lesson 1 Pattern
variants.pattern: N1 は N2 じゃありません
variants.explanation: じゃありません is the polite negative of です: "is not / am not". In formal or written contexts ではありません is used instead, with the same meaning.

examples.japanese: サントスさんは 学生じゃありません。
examples.reading: サントスさんは 学生じゃありません。
examples.meaning: Mr. Santos is not a student.

examples.japanese: サントスさんは 学生じゃありません。
examples.reading: サントスさんは 学生じゃありません。
examples.meaning: Mr. Santos is not a student.

grammarPoints.title: 第1課 • 〜ですか — questions
grammarPoints.japanese: N1 は N2 ですか
grammarPoints.explanation: To ask a question you just add the particle か at the end of the sentence; the word order does not change and Japanese uses no question mark. The intonation rises at the end. You answer with はい (yes) or いいえ (no).
grammarPoints.pattern: N1 は N2 ですか

variants.label: Lesson 1 Pattern
variants.pattern: N1 は N2 ですか
variants.explanation: To ask a question you just add the particle か at the end of the sentence; the word order does not change and Japanese uses no question mark. The intonation rises at the end. You answer with はい (yes) or いいえ (no).

examples.japanese: ミラーさんはアメリカ 人ですか。
examples.reading: ミラーさんはアメリカ 人ですか。
examples.meaning: Is Mr. Miller American?

examples.japanese: はい、アメリカ 人です。
examples.reading: はい、アメリカ 人です。
examples.meaning: Yes, he is American.

examples.japanese: ミラーさんはアメリカ 人ですか。
examples.reading: ミラーさんはアメリカ 人ですか。
examples.meaning: Is Mr. Miller American?

examples.japanese: はい、アメリカ 人です。
examples.reading: はい、アメリカ 人です。
examples.meaning: Yes, he is American.

grammarPoints.title: 第1課 • N も — "also"
grammarPoints.explanation: The particle も replaces は when what is said about the new topic is the same as what was said about the previous one: it means "also, too".
grammarPoints.pattern: N1 も N2 です

variants.label: Lesson 1 Pattern
variants.explanation: The particle も replaces は when what is said about the new topic is the same as what was said about the previous one: it means "also, too".

examples.japanese: グプタさんも 会社員です。
examples.reading: グプタさんも 会社員です。
examples.meaning: Mr. Gupta is a company employee too.

examples.japanese: グプタさんも 会社員です。
examples.reading: グプタさんも 会社員です。
examples.meaning: Mr. Gupta is a company employee too.

grammarPoints.title: 第1課 • N1 の N2 — belonging
grammarPoints.explanation: The particle の joins two nouns: the first one narrows down or classifies the second. Here it shows the organisation someone belongs to.
grammarPoints.pattern: N1 の N2

variants.label: Lesson 1 Pattern
variants.explanation: The particle の joins two nouns: the first one narrows down or classifies the second. Here it shows the organisation someone belongs to.

examples.japanese: ミラーさんはIMCの 社員です。
examples.reading: ミラーさんはIMCの 社員です。
examples.meaning: Mr. Miller is an IMC employee.

examples.japanese: ミラーさんはIMCの 社員です。
examples.reading: ミラーさんはIMCの 社員です。
examples.meaning: Mr. Miller is an IMC employee.

grammarPoints.title: 第1課 • 〜さん — respectful address
grammarPoints.explanation: さん is added to other people's surname or name to show respect; it works for men and women alike. It is never used with your own name. With small children ちゃん is used, and くん with young boys.
grammarPoints.pattern: Surname + さん

variants.label: Lesson 1 Pattern
variants.explanation: さん is added to other people's surname or name to show respect; it works for men and women alike. It is never used with your own name. With small children ちゃん is used, and くん with young boys.

examples.japanese: こちらはサントスさんです。
examples.reading: こちらはサントスさんです。
examples.meaning: This is Mr. Santos.

examples.japanese: こちらはサントスさんです。
examples.reading: こちらはサントスさんです。
examples.meaning: This is Mr. Santos.

grammarPoints.title: 第2課 • これ／それ／あれ — "this, that, that over there"
grammarPoints.japanese: これ／それ／あれ は N です
grammarPoints.explanation: These are demonstrative pronouns that work like nouns. これ points at something near the speaker, それ at something near the listener, and あれ at something far from both.
grammarPoints.pattern: これ／それ／あれ は N です

variants.label: Lesson 2 Pattern
variants.pattern: これ／それ／あれ は N です
variants.explanation: These are demonstrative pronouns that work like nouns. これ points at something near the speaker, それ at something near the listener, and あれ at something far from both.

examples.japanese: これは 辞書です。
examples.reading: これは 辞書です。
examples.meaning: This is a dictionary.

examples.japanese: それはボールペンですか。
examples.reading: それはボールペンですか。
examples.meaning: Is that a pen?

examples.japanese: これは 辞書です。
examples.reading: これは 辞書です。
examples.meaning: This is a dictionary.

examples.japanese: それはボールペンですか。
examples.reading: それはボールペンですか。
examples.meaning: Is that a pen?

examples.japanese: あれは 私のかばんです。
examples.reading: あれは 私のかばんです。
examples.meaning: That over there is my bag.

grammarPoints.title: 第2課 • この／その／あの + N — "this/that + noun"
grammarPoints.explanation: Unlike これ・それ・あれ, these forms never stand alone: they always accompany a noun. Distance works the same way: この (speaker), その (listener), あの (far from both).
grammarPoints.pattern: この／その／あの N

variants.label: Lesson 2 Pattern
variants.explanation: Unlike これ・それ・あれ, these forms never stand alone: they always accompany a noun. Distance works the same way: この (speaker), その (listener), あの (far from both).

examples.japanese: この 本は 私のです。
examples.reading: この 本は 私のです。
examples.meaning: This book is mine.

examples.japanese: あの 人は 誰ですか。
examples.reading: あの 人は 誰ですか。
examples.meaning: Who is that person over there?

examples.japanese: この 本は 私のです。
examples.reading: この 本は 私のです。
examples.meaning: This book is mine.

examples.japanese: あの 人は 誰ですか。
examples.reading: あの 人は 誰ですか。
examples.meaning: Who is that person over there?

grammarPoints.title: 第2課 • そうです — "that's right"
grammarPoints.japanese: はい、そうです ／ いいえ、そうじゃありません
grammarPoints.explanation: To answer "is N N?" questions you use そう with です: はい、そうです (yes, that's right) or いいえ、そうじゃありません (no, it isn't). You can also answer with いいえ、違[ちが]います.
grammarPoints.pattern: はい、そうです ／ いいえ、そうじゃありません

variants.label: Lesson 2 Pattern
variants.pattern: はい、そうです ／ いいえ、そうじゃありません
variants.explanation: To answer "is N N?" questions you use そう with です: はい、そうです (yes, that's right) or いいえ、そうじゃありません (no, it isn't). You can also answer with いいえ、違[ちが]います.

examples.japanese: それは 手帳ですか。…はい、そうです。
examples.reading: それは 手帳ですか。…はい、そうです。
examples.meaning: Is that a diary? …Yes, it is.

examples.japanese: それはノートですか。…いいえ、そうじゃありません。
examples.reading: それはノートですか。…いいえ、そうじゃありません。
examples.meaning: Is that a notebook? …No, it isn't.

examples.japanese: それは 手帳ですか。…はい、そうです。
examples.reading: それは 手帳ですか。…はい、そうです。
examples.meaning: Is that a diary? …Yes, it is.

examples.japanese: それはノートですか。…いいえ、そうじゃありません。
examples.reading: それはノートですか。…いいえ、そうじゃありません。
examples.meaning: Is that a notebook? …No, it isn't.

grammarPoints.title: 第2課 • 〜か、〜か — alternative questions
grammarPoints.japanese: N1 ですか、N2 ですか
grammarPoints.explanation: This offers two options and asks the listener to pick one. You do not answer with はい or いいえ, but by saying the right option directly.
grammarPoints.pattern: N1 ですか、N2 ですか

variants.label: Lesson 2 Pattern
variants.pattern: N1 ですか、N2 ですか
variants.explanation: This offers two options and asks the listener to pick one. You do not answer with はい or いいえ, but by saying the right option directly.

examples.japanese: これは「9」ですか、「7」ですか。…「9」です。
examples.reading: これは「9」ですか、「7」ですか。…「9」です。
examples.meaning: Is this a 9 or a 7? …It's a 9.

examples.japanese: これは「9」ですか、「7」ですか。…「9」です。
examples.reading: これは「9」ですか、「7」ですか。…「9」です。
examples.meaning: Is this a 9 or a 7? …It's a 9.

grammarPoints.title: 第2課 • N1 の N2 — possession and content
grammarPoints.explanation: As well as ownership (私[わたし]の 本[ほん], my book), の says what something is about: コンピューターの 本[ほん] is "a computer book".
grammarPoints.pattern: N1 の N2

variants.label: Lesson 2 Pattern
variants.explanation: As well as ownership (私[わたし]の 本[ほん], my book), の says what something is about: コンピューターの 本[ほん] is "a computer book".

examples.japanese: これはコンピューターの 本です。
examples.reading: これはコンピューターの 本です。
examples.meaning: This is a computer book.

grammarPoints.title: 第7課 • N1 (person) に N2 を もらいます — "to receive"

grammarPoints.title: 第8課 • The two kinds of adjective
grammarPoints.explanation: Japanese has -い adjectives (大[おお]きい, 高[たか]い) and -な adjectives (きれい[な], 有名[ゆうめい][な]). They behave differently when modifying nouns and when conjugating, so it pays to memorise each adjective together with its type.

grammarPoints.title: 第8課 • N は A です — the adjective as predicate
grammarPoints.japanese: N は A-な[な] です ／ N は A-い(〜い) です
grammarPoints.explanation: As a predicate, both types are followed by です. The -な adjective drops the な: 静[しず]かです. The negative differs: -な adjectives use じゃありません (静[しず]かじゃありません) and -い adjectives change 〜い to 〜くないです (高[たか]くないです). The negative of いい is よくないです.

grammarPoints.title: 第12課 • N1 と N2 と どちらが A ですか — comparing two
grammarPoints.japanese: N1 と N2 と どちらが A ですか。…N の ほうが A です
grammarPoints.explanation: To ask which of two things is more…, you use どちら, whatever the category. You answer with 〜の ほうが: サッカーと 野球[やきゅう]と どちらが おもしろいですか。…サッカーの ほうが おもしろいです. If they are equal: どちらも (both).

grammarPoints.title: 第12課 • N [の 中[なか]] で 〜が いちばん A です — superlative
grammarPoints.japanese: N [の 中[なか]]で 何[なに]／どこ／誰[だれ]／いつ が いちばん A ですか

grammarPoints.title: 第14課 • The three verb groups
grammarPoints.japanese: Group I (godan) ／ Group II (ichidan) ／ Group III (irregular)
grammarPoints.explanation: Japanese verbs fall into three groups according to how they conjugate. Group I: the syllable before ます ends in -i (書[か]きます, 飲[の]みます). Group II: it ends in -e, or in -i for a few like 見[み]ます・います (食[た]べます, 起[お]きます). Group III: します and 来[き]ます. Knowing the group is essential for building the て form.

grammarPoints.title: 第14課 • The て form
grammarPoints.japanese: 書[か]きます→書[か]いて ／ 飲[の]みます→飲[の]んで ／ 食[た]べます→食[た]べて ／ します→して
grammarPoints.explanation: In group I the ending changes with the syllable: き→いて (書[か]いて), ぎ→いで (急[いそ]いで), み・び・に→んで (飲[の]んで, 呼[よ]んで), い・ち・り→って (買[か]って, 待[ま]って, 取[と]って), し→して (話[はな]して). 行[い]きます is an exception: 行[い]って. Group II simply swaps ます for て (食[た]べて) and group III gives して・来[き]て.

grammarPoints.title: 第17課 • The ない form
grammarPoints.japanese: 書[か]きます→書[か]かない ／ 食[た]べます→食[た]べない ／ します→しない ／ 来[き]ます→来[こ]ない

grammarPoints.title: 第20課 • Polite style and plain style
grammarPoints.japanese: です・ます ↔ plain form (だ, 行[い]く, 高[たか]い…)
grammarPoints.explanation: The polite style (です・ます) is used with strangers, with superiors and in formal situations. The plain style uses the plain forms of verbs and adjectives (行[い]く, 行[い]かない, 行[い]った, 高[たか]い, 静[しず]かだ) and belongs to family and friends.

grammarPoints.title: 〜は (wa)
grammarPoints.meaning: as for; marks the topic of the sentence
grammarPoints.explanation: Written は but pronounced 'wa'. It sets up what the sentence is about; the key information comes after it. The は (wa) particle is used to indicate the topic of a sentence. grammarPoints.title: 〜も (mo)
grammarPoints.meaning: also; too; (with a negative) not ... either; neither ... nor
grammarPoints.explanation: も replaces は, が and を, but comes after other particles: 京都にも行きました. The も grammar point is used after a noun to indicate that the action or state is the same for multiple items or people. It means 'also', 'as well', or 'too' in English. も often replaces は or が in the sentence to show that the same statement applies to this additional noun.

grammarPoints.title: 〜です (desu)
grammarPoints.explanation: Forms: です, ではありません, でした, ではありませんでした. After an い-adjective, です only adds politeness: 高いです. です links a subject to a predicate noun or na-adjective as the polite form of だ. It appears at the end of polite sentences and is the single most characteristic word of polite Japanese speech. です does not conjugate like a verb; tense and negation are expressed through its auxiliary forms (でした, ではありません, ではありませんでした).

grammarPoints.title: 〜だ (da)
grammarPoints.explanation: Forms: だ, じゃない, だった, じゃなかった. Never used right after an い-adjective (高いだ is wrong). Often dropped in casual questions: 学生？ だ is the plain-form copula, used in casual speech, writing, and when attaching copular predicates to grammatical constructions that require the plain form (e.g., before と in quotation or before から in giving reasons). In feminine and neutral speech だ is often dropped at the end of standalone sentences.

grammarPoints.title: 〜て (te)
grammarPoints.meaning: and; and then (linking actions in order)
grammarPoints.explanation: The final verb sets the tense for the whole sentence. 書く→書いて, 飲む→飲んで, 話す→話して, 買う→買って, 行く→行って (irregular). The ～て form of a verb is used to connect actions or states in a sequence, implying that the first action is completed before the second one starts. The ～て form is frequently used in casual speech, and it can also be used in polite speech when combined with certain auxiliary verbs like ください (kudasai) or いる (iru).

grammarPoints.title: 〜てから (te kara)
grammarPoints.meaning: after doing; (do A) and then (B); since
grammarPoints.explanation: Stresses that A is finished before B starts, more clearly than a plain て. With ている in the main clause it often means 'since'. The ～てから grammar point is used to indicate the sequence of actions or events, meaning that one action or event occurs after another. It can be translated as 'after', 'since', or 'once' in English. The て-form indicates the first action and から shows the sequence.

grammarPoints.title: これ / それ / あれ / どれ (kore / sore / are / dore)
grammarPoints.japanese: これ / それ / あれ / どれ
grammarPoints.meaning: this one; that one (near you); that one (over there); which one
grammarPoints.explanation: こ = near the speaker, そ = near the listener, あ = away from both, ど = question. They stand alone; as a subject どれ takes が, not は. これ refers to something near the speaker, それ to something near the listener (or already mentioned), あれ to something far from both, and どれ asks 'which one?'. This three-way distance distinction (ko-so-a-do system) pervades Japanese demonstratives. These forms stand alone as pronouns; the parallel attributive forms この/その/あの/どの precede a noun.

variants.explanation: こ = near the speaker, そ = near the listener, あ = away from both, ど = question. They stand alone; as a subject どれ takes が, not は. これ refers to something near the speaker, それ to something near the listener (or already mentioned), あれ to something far from both, and どれ asks 'which one?'. This three-way distance distinction (ko-so-a-do system) pervades Japanese demonstratives. These forms stand alone as pronouns; the parallel attributive forms この/その/あの/どの precede a noun.

grammarPoints.japanese: この / その / あの / どの
grammarPoints.meaning: this; that (near you); that ... over there; which (before a noun)
grammarPoints.explanation: Always followed by a noun: この本, never この alone. これ / それ / あれ / どれ are used when there is no noun. これ/それ/あれ/どれ stand alone as pronouns; この/その/あの/どの attach directly before a noun to modify it, like English 'this/that/which' + noun. grammarPoints.explanation: こちら / そちら / あちら / どちら are politer versions: お国はどちらですか (Where are you from?). grammarPoints.title: 〜てあげる (te ageru)

The てあげる grammar point is used to express that the speaker or someone other than the listener is doing something for someone else. grammarPoints.meaning: someone does something for me (or my group)
grammarPoints.explanation: The subject is the person doing the favor; the one who benefits is the speaker or someone close to them. The て くれる grammar point is used to express when someone does something for, or gives something to the speaker (or someone in the speaker's group). The action is usually done willingly or as a favor by the person performing the action. It is usually translated into English as 'to do something for me' or 'to give something to me'.

grammarPoints.title: 〜てある (te aru)
grammarPoints.meaning: has been done (and stays that way); resulting state of a deliberate action
grammarPoints.explanation: Used with transitive verbs, and the object usually takes が. It implies someone did it on purpose, unlike 〜ている with intransitive verbs (窓が開いている). The ～てある grammar point is used to express that an action has been done and its result remains in effect. It indicates that the action was intentionally performed and its effect continues. The formation is done by conjugating the verb into its て-form and then adding ある.

grammarPoints.title: 〜方 (kata)
grammarPoints.explanation: The result is a noun, so the object takes の instead of を (日本語の話し方). With する-verbs: 勉強のしかた. The ～方 grammar point is used to express the way or method of doing something, similar to 'how to' or 'the way of' in English. It can be attached to the stem of a verb to form a noun that indicates the method of doing the action. In practice, ～方 is usually read as '～かた' (e.g., 作り方＝つくりかた).

grammarPoints.title: 〜中 (chuu / juu)
grammarPoints.meaning: in the middle of; during (ちゅう); throughout; all over (じゅう)
grammarPoints.explanation: ちゅう marks an ongoing activity or a period (会議中, 午前中, 今週中); じゅう means 'throughout' a time or place (一日中, 世界中). The 中 (ちゅう) grammar point is used to express that something is in the middle of, during, or in the process of happening. It is attached to a noun to convey this meaning (e.g., 勉強中, 仕事中, 会議中). It is also sometimes read as じゅう depending on the word (e.g., 授業中).

grammarPoints.explanation: Softer than the imperative form but still a firm instruction; used by parents, teachers and in exam directions, never toward superiors. grammarPoints.title: 〜ても / 〜でも (te mo / de mo)
grammarPoints.explanation: With question words or いくら it means 'no matter ...' (何を食べても, いくら待っても). grammarPoints.title: 〜ために (tame ni)
grammarPoints.meaning: in order to; for (the sake of); because of
grammarPoints.explanation: For purpose, the verb must be something the subject can control (compare 〜ように). The 'because of' use sounds fairly formal. The ために (tame ni) grammar point is used to express either the purpose of doing something (in which case it translates to 'for the sake of' or 'in order to') or the cause/reason for a situation (in which case it translates to 'because of'). Typically, we use the dictionary form of the verb (e.g., 合格する) for the 'in order to' meaning. For an adjective or noun, attach ために appropriately (い-Adjective + ために, な-Adjective + な + ために, Noun + の + ために).

grammarPoints.explanation: 〜ようにしている describes a habit you keep up. Compare 〜ようになる, a change that comes about. grammarPoints.title: 〜かもしれない (kamo shirenai)
grammarPoints.explanation: About 50% certainty or less. In casual speech it is often shortened to かも. The ～かもしれない grammar point is used to express uncertainty or the possibility of something occurring. It can be translated as 'maybe', 'might', or 'possibly' in English. The formation differs depending on whether it is used with a verb, い-adjective, な-adjective, or noun. In everyday speech, speakers often omit だ before かもしれない for nouns and な-adjectives.

The ばかり grammar point is used to express that something is only, nothing but, just, or always. It can be attached to nouns, verbs, or adjectives, and has various meanings based on the context.

grammarPoints.title: 〜出す (dasu)
grammarPoints.explanation: Implies a sudden, often uncontrolled start. Unlike 〜始める, it is not used for planned actions or in requests. The verb 出す (~dasu) is used to express the action of taking something out, starting an action, or emphasizing the verb it is attached to. To form this grammar point, simply attach 出す (~dasu) to the stem of the verb.

grammarPoints.title: 〜までに (made ni)
grammarPoints.explanation: までに marks a deadline for a one-time action; まで marks how long something continues (六時まで働く). The ～までに grammar point is used to indicate that something must be completed or occurs by a certain time or before a specific action. It can be used with verbs, nouns, and time expressions.

grammarPoints.title: 〜させてください (sasete kudasai)
grammarPoints.explanation: Built on the causative て-form (する → させて). 〜させていただけませんか is more polite. The ～させてください grammar point is used to make a polite request to allow or permit someone to do something. It can be translated as 'please let me' or 'please allow me to' in English. It is formed by taking the causative form of a verb and adding ください.

grammarPoints.title: 〜かな / 〜かしら (kana / kashira)
grammarPoints.explanation: A soft question, often said to oneself. かしら sounds feminine and a little old-fashioned. 〜ないかな can express a wish (早く来ないかな).
grammarPoints.pattern: Verb-plain / i-Adj / na-Adj / Noun + かな / かしら

grammarPoints.title: 〜てくれませんか / 〜ていただけませんか (te kuremasen ka / te itadakemasen ka)
grammarPoints.japanese: 〜てくれませんか / 〜ていただけませんか
grammarPoints.romaji: te kuremasen ka / te itadakemasen ka
grammarPoints.explanation: Softer than 〜てください. Politeness rises from 〜てくれませんか to 〜てもらえませんか to 〜ていただけませんか.
